question:
Patient note:
A 62-year-old man with a background of insulin-dependent type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease treated with a long-acting bronchodilator, stage 3 chronic kidney disease, and remote alcohol use disorder was transported to our emergency department from a skilled-nursing facility after staff noted a sudden decline in responsiveness accompanied by labored breathing and a recorded fever of 38.9 °C; he had completed a five-day course of oral levofloxacin for presumed bronchitis one week earlier but never fully returned to baseline energy. According to the transfer paperwork, he ambulated with a walker the day before but spoke in single words and appeared confused on the morning of presentation. Paramedics found him slumped over the side rails of his bed, moaning but without purposeful movement, saturating 82 % on room air. They applied a high-concentration Venturi mask set to deliver 55 % inspired oxygen and transported him in a semi-upright position; no sedation, paralytic agents, or advanced airway devices were used en route, and there were no intravenous fluids started in the field. Ten minutes after arrival in our resuscitation bay—before any antibiotic, crystalloid bolus, or vasoactive infusion had been administered—his vital signs revealed a heart rate of 124 beats per minute in sinus tachycardia, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute with shallow excursions, temperature 39.2 °C, and a cuff blood pressure repeatedly measured at 84/44 mm Hg with a mean in the mid-50s. Peripheral pulses were faint, capillary refill exceeded four seconds, and the skin of the distal extremities was mottled and cool to touch. An arterial blood sample drawn from the right radial artery while he remained on 55 % FiO₂ yielded a PaO₂ of 88 mm Hg, PaCO₂ 42 mm Hg, pH 7.31, bicarbonate 20 mEq/L, and lactate 4.6 mmol/L. On neurologic examination he did not open his eyes to voice or to nail-bed pressure, emitted only guttural incomprehensible sounds, and demonstrated bilateral extension at the elbows with internal rotation of the shoulders when the sternum was rubbed, for a composite Glasgow Coma Score of 5; pupils were 4 mm and sluggish but symmetric, corneal reflexes were present, and there was no lateralizing deficit. Auscultation of the chest disclosed coarse inspiratory crackles over the right lower two thirds and scattered wheezes bilaterally, while percussion was dull over the same right basilar segment. Cardiac examination showed a rapid regular rhythm without murmurs, jugular venous pressure was not appreciable in the sitting position, and the abdomen was soft with mild epigastric tenderness but no guarding. A bedside bladder scan after Foley insertion registered minimal volume, and the initial catheter drainage produced only 30 mL of dark amber urine; review of the facility flow sheet handed to the triage nurse documented an aggregate urinary output of 700 mL during the preceding twenty-four hours. Initial laboratory studies obtained from the first venipuncture demonstrated a white blood cell count of 21.3 × 10³/µL with 15 % bands, hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL, hematocrit 37 %, and a platelet count of 110 000/µL. Serum chemistry panel returned sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 4.9 mmol/L, chloride 99 mmol/L, bicarbonate 19 mmol/L, glucose 198 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 52 mg/dL, and a creatinine of 2.2 mg/dL, representing a clear rise from his documented baseline of 1.5 mg/dL two months earlier. Hepatic indices revealed total bilirubin 1.4 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase 58 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 44 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase 136 U/L; coagulation profile showed an international normalized ratio of 1.6 and activated partial thromboplastin time 45 seconds. High-sensitivity troponin I was 0.05 ng/mL, and procalcitonin measured 38 ng/mL. A portable anteroposterior chest radiograph taken within fifteen minutes of arrival demonstrated a dense right lower-lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small adjacent pleural effusion but no obvious cardiomegaly. Computed tomography of the head without contrast, performed promptly because of the depressed sensorium, revealed only chronic microvascular changes without hemorrhage or mass effect. The patient’s medication list included metformin (held at the facility because of poor oral intake), glargine insulin, tiotropium inhaler, and low-dose aspirin; he was not receiving corticosteroids or anticoagulation, and nursing notes denied recent nephrotoxic exposures. He consumed alcohol socially in the distant past, had quit smoking ten years ago after a twenty-pack-year history, and had no known drug allergies. The working impression on arrival favored severe community-acquired pneumonia with systemic inflammatory response, progressing to distributive shock, acute encephalopathy, evolving acute kidney injury on chronic disease, and early consumptive thrombocytopenia. Airway protection, aggressive fluid resuscitation, broad-spectrum antimicrobials, and possible vasopressor support were all discussed with the attending physician, but at the moment the data above were captured the patient remained breathing spontaneously through the 55 % oxygen mask, still profoundly obtunded and hypotensive, without having yet received any therapeutic intervention in our emergency department.

Question: What is the patient's Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) Score?
solution:
The Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) sums six organ-system subscores, each ranging from 0 to 4. Using the presentation data:
- Respiratory: PaO₂/FiO₂ = 88/0.55 = 160 mm Hg. The ratio is <300, and he is breathing spontaneously on a mask without ventilatory support: 2 points.
- Coagulation: Platelets 110,000/µL are in the 100,000–149,999/µL range: 1 point.
- Liver: Total bilirubin 1.4 mg/dL is in the 1.2–1.9 range: 1 point.
- Cardiovascular: MAP ≈ (84 + 2 × 44)/3 = 57 mm Hg, below 70 without vasopressors: 1 point.
- Neurologic: GCS 5 is below 6: 4 points.
- Renal: Creatinine 2.2 mg/dL is in the 2.0–3.4 range: 2 points. Urine output of 700 mL over 24 hours does not meet the <500 mL/day threshold for a higher score.
Total = 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 4 + 2 = 11.
Final answer: 11
